source: Original (freshly authored 2026-09-15, HL syllabus 1.14, no calculator). de Moivre at n = 3 plus the binomial expansion, equating real parts to derive the triple-angle identity cos 3t = 4cos^3 t - 3cos t. Problems 1 and 2 are a single 'hence' chain split across two pages so each has a full page of working space.

parts.label: a
parts.description: Use de Moivre's theorem to write (cos t + i sin t)^3 in terms of cos 3t and sin 3t.

expected.answer: (cos t + i sin t)^3 = cos 3t + i sin 3t

parts.tolerance: Accept cis 3t or e^(3it) written alongside the required form. Accept the general statement of de Moivre followed by the substitution n = 3.
parts.notes: A1 for a correct statement at n = 3. The right-hand side must show both cos 3t and i sin 3t.

parts.label: b
parts.description: Expand (cos t + i sin t)^3 by the binomial theorem, simplifying the powers of i.

expected.answer: cos^3 t + 3i cos^2 t sin t - 3 cos t sin^2 t - i sin^3 t

parts.tolerance: Accept any arrangement, and accept the real and imaginary parts collected or left in the order of the expansion. Accept Pascal's triangle coefficients written out.
parts.notes: M1 for a complete four-term expansion with coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1. A1 for simplifying i^2 = -1 and i^3 = -i correctly. An expansion that leaves i^2 unevaluated earns the M1 only.

parts.label: c
parts.description: By equating real parts, show that cos 3t = 4 cos^3 t - 3 cos t. (Answer given.)

expected.answer: cos 3t = cos^3 t - 3 cos t sin^2 t = cos^3 t - 3 cos t (1 - cos^2 t) = 4 cos^3 t - 3 cos t

parts.tolerance: Show that (answer given). Accept the Pythagorean substitution written as sin^2 t = 1 - cos^2 t or as 1 - sin^2 t = cos^2 t.
parts.notes: M1 for equating the real part of (a) with the real part of (b). A1 for using sin^2 t = 1 - cos^2 t to remove the sine. AG for reaching the printed result. Both preceding lines must be present: a candidate who writes the identity down from memory earns nothing, since the result is given.

source: Original (freshly authored 2026-09-15, HL syllabus 1.14 with trigonometric equation solving). Continues the chain from Problem 1: imaginary parts give sin 3t = 3 sin t - 4 sin^3 t, then 8cos^3 t - 6cos t = 2 cos 3t turns a cubic into cos 3t = 1/2, with solutions t = pi/9, 5pi/9, 7pi/9 on [0, pi).

parts.label: a
parts.description: Equate imaginary parts to find sin 3t in terms of sin t only.
parts.tolerance: Accept the terms in either order. The expression must be in sin t alone.
parts.notes: M1 for equating the imaginary parts of the two expressions from Problem 1. A1 for the expression in sin t only. Stopping at 3 cos^2 t sin t - sin^3 t earns the M1 only, because the question asks for sin t alone.

parts.label: b
parts.description: Hence solve 8 cos^3 t - 6 cos t = 1 for 0 <= t < pi, giving exact multiples of pi.
parts.tolerance: Accept the three solutions in any order. Exact multiples of pi only; decimals earn nothing for the final mark.
parts.notes: M1 for recognising 8cos^3 t - 6cos t as 2(4cos^3 t - 3cos t) = 2 cos 3t and reducing to cos 3t = 1/2 - this is what 'hence' asks for. A1 for all three values of 3t in the widened interval [0, 3pi); finding only 3t = pi/3 loses this mark, and that is the commonest error. A1 for the three values of t. A candidate who solves the cubic numerically or graphically earns nothing on this part.
parts.follow_through: Award the final A1 for the candidate's own values of 3t each correctly divided by 3, even when the set of 3t values is incomplete or wrong.

source: Original (freshly authored 2026-09-15, HL syllabus 1.14). Fifth roots of unity: z = e^(2k pi i/5) for k = 0, +/-1, +/-2, giving arguments 0, +/-2pi/5, +/-4pi/5 inside -pi < theta <= pi; the roots sum to zero and form a regular pentagon on the unit circle with one vertex at z = 1. An unlabelled Argand grid is printed for optional working.

parts.label: a
parts.description: Find all five solutions of z^5 = 1 in the form e^(i theta) with -pi < theta <= pi.
parts.tolerance: Accept cis form throughout. Accept e^(0i) or 1 for the first root. Arguments must lie in -pi < theta <= pi: e^(6 pi i/5) and e^(8 pi i/5) are outside the range and must be converted.
parts.notes: M1 for writing 1 as e^(2k pi i) with the 2k pi allowance shown or used, and taking fifth roots. First A1 for modulus 1 together with any one correct non-zero argument. Second A1 for all five roots with every argument inside the stated range. Giving the roots as k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 without converting the last two into the required range loses the second A1 only.

parts.label: b
parts.description: Show that the five solutions sum to zero.

expected.answer: The five roots are the roots of z^5 - 1 = 0, whose z^4 coefficient is 0, so the sum of the roots is 0.

parts.tolerance: Accept any complete argument: sum of roots from the coefficients; the geometric series 1 + w + w^2 + w^3 + w^4 = (1 - w^5)/(1 - w) = 0 for w not equal to 1; or five unit vectors equally spaced by 2pi/5 cancelling.
parts.notes: R1 for a complete reason. 'They cancel by symmetry' with nothing further earns nothing: the equal spacing, or the algebra, has to be stated. Numerically adding decimal approximations of the five roots earns nothing, since the question says show.

parts.label: c
parts.description: Describe the figure formed on an Argand diagram, stating its centre and the distance of each vertex from the origin.

expected.answer: A regular pentagon centred at the origin, with each vertex a distance 1 from the origin (on the unit circle), one vertex at z = 1 and consecutive vertices 2pi/5 apart.

parts.tolerance: Accept 'regular pentagon' or 'regular 5-sided polygon'. Accept 'radius 1' or 'on the unit circle' for the distance.
parts.notes: A1 requires the pentagon together with both requested details: centre at the origin and vertices at distance 1. 'A pentagon' alone earns nothing, and neither does 'a regular polygon' without the number of sides.
